paper.title: Known Unknowns: Out-of-Distribution Property Prediction in Materials and Molecules
paper.research_summary: Our objective is to train predictor models that extrapolate zero-shot to higher ranges than in the training data, given the chemical compositions of solids or molecular graphs and their property values. We propose using a transductive approach to OOD property prediction, achieving improvements in prediction accuracy. In particular, our method improves extrapolative precision by 1.8× for materials and 1.5× for molecules, and boosts recall of high-performing candidates by up to 3×. Our method leverages analogical input-target relations in the training and test sets, enabling generalization beyond the training target support, and can be applied to any other material and molecular tasks.

tasks.objective: Train predictor models that extrapolate zero-shot to higher ranges than in the training data, given the chemical compositions of solids or molecular graphs and their property values.
constraints: property values outside the known distribution
zero-shot extrapolation to unseen property value ranges beyond the training distribution
output_goal: predicted property values for out-of-distribution (OOD) samples

evidence.text: Our objective is to train predictor models that extrapolate zero-shot to higher ranges than in the training data, given the chemical compositions of solids or molecular graphs and their property values.

We focus on predicting property values from materials representations and exploring zero-shot extrapolation, i.e., evaluating the model on unseen property value ranges beyond the training distribution.

stages.stage_name_raw: Curating benchmark datasets for solids and molecules
stages.stage_goal: Acquire diverse, high-throughput computational and experimental datasets covering solid-state materials and molecules.

evidence.text: We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.

For molecular systems, we used datasets from MoleculeNet, covering four graph-to-property prediction tasks with dataset sizes ranging from 600 to 4200 samples, and benchmarked our approach against three baseline methods.

stages.stage_goal: Convert raw material compositions and molecular graphs into fixed descriptor-based representations suitable for modeling.

evidence.text: Let X ⊂ Rn denote a representation space of data points, such as RDKit descriptors derived from Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) for molecules, and the composition-based descriptors Oliynyk27 derived from elemental properties for solids.
Specifically, for solids, we focus on compositionally driven variation in properties and utilize stoichiometry-based representations.

stages.stage_name_raw: Defining OOD labels via top/bottom percentile thresholds
stages.stage_goal: Identify out-of-distribution (OOD) samples by selecting extreme property value ranges not present in training data.
stage_output: OOD test set (top 5% highest property values)
ID validation set (random 5% of remaining data)

evidence.text: We split the data into training, validation and test sets such that OOD test samples Dte_Y ⊂ Y are 5% of the data with the highest property values, an ID validation set is a random sample of 5% of the remaining data, and the training set Dtr = {(x, y)}n ⊂ X × Y is the rest.
If, instead, the goal were to identify materials with exceptionally low property values, we could redefine OOD samples as the bottom 5% rather than the top 5%.

stages.stage_goal: Train a bilinear transductive predictor hθ(Δx, x) = fθ(Δx)gθ(x) to learn how property values change as a function of material differences.
stage_input: training set Dtr = {(x, y)}n ⊂ X × Y
differences distribution ΔX = {xi − xj | xi, xj ∈ X}

evidence.text: During training, rather than predicting hθ : X → Y, predictor hθ : ΔX × X → Y predicts value y2 ∈ Dtr_Y for data point x2 ∈ Dtr_X given anchor point x1 ∈ Dtr_X and the difference between them Δx21 = x2 − x1 ∈ Dtr_ΔX.
The predictor hθ(Δx, x) = fθ(Δx)gθ(x) is implemented as a bilinear function in non-linear embeddings of Δx and x.

stages.stage_name_raw: Screening for top OOD candidates using extrapolative precision
stages.stage_goal: Identify high-performing OOD candidates by selecting top predicted property values and evaluating fraction of true top OOD candidates correctly identified.

evidence.text: In addition, we report model performance on a purely extrapolative task of discovering high-performance extremes: identifying the 30% of test samples with the highest property values, which we refer to as the top OOD candidates (Table 2). This is quantified by extrapolative precision, which measures the fraction of true top OOD candidates correctly identified among the model’s top predicted OOD candidates.

stages.stage_name_raw: Evaluating OOD prediction accuracy and distributional alignment
stages.stage_goal: Quantify model performance on OOD samples using mean absolute error (MAE), recall, and kernel density estimation (KDE) overlap.

evidence.text: Table 1 presents the mean absolute error (MAE) for OOD predictions on solids, showing that Bilinear Transduction consistently outperforms or performs comparably to the baseline methods across tasks.
Bilinear Transduction boosts recall of OOD materials by 3 ×, compared with the best average recall score among the models presented in Table S2.
As a quantitative metric, the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) overlap reported in Supplementary Material 1.1.3 conﬁrms this improved alignment.

We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.

Matbench is an automated leaderboard for benchmarking ML algorithms predicting solid material properties12. Matbench contains three composition-based regression tasks: experimentally measured band gap14, experimentally measured yield strength of steels31, calculated formation energy32, and calculated refractive index33.

We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.
MP provides materials and their property values derived from high-throughput calculations32.

For molecular systems, we used datasets from MoleculeNet, covering four graph-to-property prediction tasks with dataset sizes ranging from 600 to 4200 samples, and benchmarked our approach against three baseline methods.
MoleculeNet includes molecular graphs encoded as SMILES representations35 and their property values derived from high-throughput calculations and experimental trials36.

The ESOL dataset provides measurements of aqueous solubility for small molecules, FreeSolv contains experimental and calculated hydration free energies for small neutral molecules in water, Lipophilicity reports octanol/water distribution coefﬁcients, and BACE includes binding afﬁnities of small molecules to human β-secretase 1 (BACE-1).
